clue.text: On the way eating cold Beef Wellington served thus

indicators.note: something eating takes food inside it, so one piece swallows the other

parts.note: French phrase used in English for travelling along
C is the standard abbreviation for cold, as on taps

explanation.surface: A traveller grabs a cold slice of beef Wellington on the go.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is a French cookery phrase meaning 'in a crust'; the French for on the way, with the abbreviation for cold inside, gives it.
explanation.definitionFit: Beef Wellington is fillet baked wrapped in pastry, which French cookery calls cooking in a crust.

clue.text: What about ten beer blow out?

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece goes round another

parts.note: eh? is said when you didn't hear, like what?
X is the Roman numeral for ten
ale is a kind of beer

explanation.surface: A drinker asks what happened to ten beers, wondering whether there will be a blowout.
explanation.walkthrough: 'What' is the questioning exclamation, not a pronoun; 'blow out' is the definition, not a binge.
explanation.definitionFit: To breathe out air from the lungs is to expel it, a phrasal synonym for this verb.

clue.text: One working to get deliveries moving off the seam down under?

definitions.text: One working to get deliveries moving off the seam down under?

parts.words: One working to get deliveries moving off the seam
parts.note: surface reading: a cricket bowler making the ball swerve off its stitched seam, perhaps in Australia (down under); setter's reading: a worker who digs fuel out of an underground seam so it can be delivered

explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a bowler's deliveries move off the seam, and 'down under' means Australia; here the seam is a layer of fuel and down under means underground.
explanation.definitionFit: This worker hews fuel from seams deep underground, from which coal is delivered to customers.

clue.text: Concerning: black substance emptied into Great Lake

parts.note: on as in about or regarding
tar is a black sticky substance

indicators.note: emptied removes the contents, leaving only the outside letters of the word

parts.note: first and last letters of into

explanation.surface: A worry that black pollution is being dumped into one of the Great Lakes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Into' looks like a link word but it is the word that is emptied.
explanation.definitionFit: This is one of the five Great Lakes of North America, on the US-Canada border.

clue.text: Sailor drowsy, exhausted, sluggish

parts.note: tar is old slang for a sailor

indicators.note: exhausted means emptied out, so only the outer letters remain

parts.note: first and last letters of drowsy

explanation.surface: A sleepy, worn-out sailor moves slowly.
explanation.definitionFit: Slow to act and late in arriving, this adjective describes delayed, slow behaviour.

clue.text: Respect initially exploratory encounters on the rebound

indicators.note: initially points to the opening letter of the word that follows

parts.note: first letter of exploratory

indicators.note: something on the rebound bounces back, so the word is read in the opposite direction

parts.note: encounters as a verb: comes across

explanation.surface: Someone on the rebound from a breakup treats first dates with careful regard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Encounters' looks like a noun for dates but is the verb meaning comes across.
explanation.definitionFit: To hold someone in high regard is to admire them, a direct synonym when both words are used as nouns or verbs.

clue.text: Kips after school? Too much of this perhaps

definitions.text: Kips after school? Too much of this perhaps

indicators.note: after places one word following another in the order they are joined

parts.note: Sch. is the abbreviation for school
kips is British slang for sleeps

explanation.surface: Pupils nod off after school, perhaps from drinking too much.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition too: too much of this strong spirit sends you to sleep.
explanation.definitionFit: This strong clear spirit, drunk in excess, leads to sleeping it off, which the clue describes.

clue.text: Bar opening in Exeter turning over loads of dosh

indicators.note: the opening of a word is its first letter

parts.note: first letter of Exeter

indicators.note: turning something over flips it, so the word reads backwards

parts.note: pots of money means a great deal of it; dosh is British slang for cash

explanation.surface: A bar opening in Exeter takes in lots of cash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bar' suggests a pub opening, but it is the legal verb.
explanation.definitionFit: In law, to be precluded from asserting something is to be barred, the verb sense of this legal term.

clue.text: Playmaker Portugal left out, playing rubbish

indicators.note: playing means fooling about, so the remaining letters are rearranged
left out means the letter for Portugal is omitted from playmaker

parts.note: P is the international vehicle registration letter for Portugal

explanation.surface: A football report: Portugal's creative midfielder has been dropped and the team is playing badly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'left out' looks like a team-sheet phrase, but it removes P (Portugal) from PLAYMAKER to leave LAYMAKER, which 'playing' rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: Malarkey is informal for nonsense or foolish talk, which is rubbish in the sense of drivel.

clue.text: Stolid Offa, dyke-builder, turned up carrying flower

indicators.note: turned up means read upwards, which in a down clue reverses the letters
carrying means holding within, so the answer sits inside these words

parts.note: the letters run across stolid, Offa and the start of dyke

explanation.surface: The stolid Anglo-Saxon king Offa, builder of the great dyke, shows up with a flower.
explanation.walkthrough: Offa was an eighth-century king of Mercia who built Offa's Dyke, the earthwork along the Welsh border. 'carrying' gives LIDOFFAD within the words, and 'turned up' reverses it.
explanation.definitionFit: The daffodil is a yellow spring bulb flower, the trumpet-shaped narcissus.

clue.text: Lonely accommodation for The King?

definitions.meaning: surface reading: a sad, isolated place to stay
setter's reading: The King is Elvis Presley, and this is the title of his 1956 hit about a lonely hotel

explanation.walkthrough: The King is the usual nickname of Elvis Presley; his song is set at a hotel 'down at the end of Lonely Street'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Elvis song title names a fictional hotel where the broken-hearted go to be lonely.

clue.text: Bloodsucker starts to lick and munch its victim

indicators.note: starts of words means taking the opening letter of each of the following words

parts.note: first letters of lick, and, munch
the creature a predator hunts

explanation.surface: A vampire-like creature licks and chews at whatever it has caught.
explanation.definitionFit: This eel-like jawless fish attaches to other fish with a sucker mouth and feeds on their blood.

clue.text: Florida paper sacking American woman in the Twenties

parts.note: Fla. is the traditional abbreviation for the US state of Florida

indicators.note: sacking someone gets rid of them, so a letter is dismissed from the word

parts.note: taken as written
A is a standard abbreviation for American

explanation.surface: A Florida newspaper fires its American woman reporter back in the 1920s.
explanation.walkthrough: Florida's older abbreviation is used here rather than the postal code FL.
explanation.definitionFit: A flapper was a fashionable, unconventional young woman of the 1920s jazz age, with bobbed hair and short dresses.

clue.text: Distinguished naked Beatle left in bed

indicators.note: naked means stripped of its covering, so the outside letters of the Beatle are removed

parts.note: John Lennon was one of the four Beatles

indicators.note: in means the letter for left is put inside the word bed

explanation.surface: A Beatle, famously naked in bed for a peace protest, is honoured.
explanation.walkthrough: 'naked' strips LENNON to ENNO, and 'in' places L (left) inside BED to make BLED, which follows. The surface recalls John Lennon's 1969 'bed-in' with Yoko Ono.
explanation.definitionFit: To be ennobled is to be raised to the nobility, which makes someone distinguished or honoured.

clue.text: Say a few words for operatic composer?

definitions.text: Say a few words for operatic composer?

parts.words: Say a few words for operatic composer
parts.note: surface reading: give a short speech in honour of a composer; setter's reading: the written text of an opera, which the composer sets to music

explanation.walkthrough: The Italian word literally means 'little book', and an opera's text is often short.
explanation.definitionFit: The text of an opera, written by a librettist, gives the composer the words to set to music.

clue.text: Move stealthily from small Python?

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
Eric Idle was a member of the Monty Python comedy team

explanation.surface: A little snake slithers away quietly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Python' suggests a snake, which fits moving stealthily, but it is the comedian Eric Idle of Monty Python.
explanation.definitionFit: To edge along furtively or sideways, trying not to be noticed, is a synonym of creeping.

clue.text: Democrat, increasingly eccentric, gin sozzled, infirm

parts.note: D is the abbreviation for Democrat

indicators.note: sozzled means very drunk, so these letters stagger into a new order

parts.note: more strange
every letter is used

explanation.surface: An ageing Democrat politician grows stranger and more unsteady, drunk on gin.
explanation.definitionFit: Shaky and trembling from old age, the adjective describes someone frail and unsteady.

clue.text: In Paris, to go rolling fag is likely to get a nasty reaction

definitions.text: likely to get a nasty reaction

parts.note: aller is French for to go

indicators.note: rolling over turns something round, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: fag is British slang for a cigarette, as is cig

explanation.surface: In Paris, going out to roll a cigarette may provoke a bad response.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rolling' a fag suggests making a roll-up cigarette; here it turns the word round.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone sensitive to a substance suffers a bad bodily response such as sneezing or a rash.

clue.text: Glaringly bright student university expelled

parts.note: L is a learner, as on British learner-driver plates
U is the abbreviation for university
got rid of, thrown out

explanation.surface: A garish story of a student thrown out of university.
explanation.definitionFit: Harsh, vivid colours that are shockingly intense are commonly described with this adjective.

clue.text: Socialite goes round boat on wide, dodgy surfing area

indicators.note: going round something encircles it, so one piece is placed outside the others

parts.note: a deb, short for debutante, is a young upper-class woman entering society
Noah's vessel
W is the cricket scoring abbreviation for a wide

explanation.surface: A socialite sails a boat out to a stretch of water with risky surfing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Surfing' suggests waves, but it means browsing the internet.
explanation.definitionFit: This hidden part of the internet, reachable only with special software, hosts much illicit activity.

clue.text: Venerable monk touring Liguria regularly spent capital

indicators.note: touring goes around a place, so one piece surrounds the other

parts.note: the Venerable Bede, the Anglo-Saxon monk and historian

indicators.note: every other letter is spent or used up at regular intervals, leaving the alternate ones

parts.note: first, third, fifth and seventh letters of Liguria

explanation.surface: An old monk on a trip through the Italian Riviera region runs out of money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spent capital' reads as used-up money, but capital is the definition and spent belongs to the letter selection.
explanation.definitionFit: This city is the capital of Serbia, formerly also of Yugoslavia.

clue.text: Embarrassed to tour near Barking — have a car crash

indicators.note: touring goes around, so one piece surrounds another

parts.note: red in the face with embarrassment

indicators.note: barking means mad, so these letters go crazy and change order

parts.note: every letter is used

explanation.surface: A red-faced driver on a trip near Barking, in east London, has a collision.
explanation.walkthrough: Barking looks like the east London place name but signals madness.
explanation.definitionFit: To drive into the back of another vehicle is a common type of collision, used here as a verb.

clue.text: Most valuable grand antique René uncovered

parts.note: G is short for a grand, a thousand pounds
old, very aged

indicators.note: uncovering strips off the outer layer, leaving only the middle letters

parts.note: middle letters of René

explanation.surface: A French dealer reveals his most prized antique.
explanation.definitionFit: Something treasured above all, like a golden opportunity or golden boy, is of the highest worth.

clue.text: Garden forceps, gripping implement

indicators.note: the phrase grips the answer, holding it within its letters

parts.note: found spanning the two words

explanation.surface: A pair of garden forceps is a handy tool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Implement' looks like a noun for a tool, which suits forceps, but here it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To put a law or rule into effect is to carry it out, the verb sense of implement.

clue.text: Ballet position which sounds like something cheesy from Switzerland?

indicators.note: the clue says outright that the answer is spoken the same as the dish that follows

parts.note: a Swiss dish of melted cheese into which bread is dipped

explanation.surface: A dancer strikes a pose that is a bit cheesy, like a Swiss dish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cheesy' in the surface means corny, but the setter means literally made of cheese.
explanation.definitionFit: In classical dance this term names a movement where the supporting leg bends at the knee, from French for melted.

clue.text: Replace bottles filled with harmless medicine

indicators.note: the words are filled with the answer, carrying it inside them

parts.note: found spanning the two words

explanation.surface: A pharmacist swaps bottles of medicine for ones with something harmless inside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bottles' looks like the containment signal, but it supplies letters; 'filled with' is the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A dummy pill with no active ingredient, given for its psychological effect, is inert and so does no harm.

clue.text: Flatbread? Mine, thanks

parts.note: a pit is a coal mine
ta is informal British for thank you

explanation.surface: Someone claims the flatbread with a polite thank-you.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mine' looks like a possessive grabbing the bread, but it is a pit.
explanation.definitionFit: This oval Middle Eastern bread, which opens into a pocket, is a type of flat leavened loaf.

clue.text: Eight down hint: we shot a classic movie

indicators.note: something shot is ruined or wrecked, so these letters are broken and rearranged

parts.note: every letter of these words is used

explanation.surface: A cross-reference to another clue offers a hint, then the film is shot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eight down' looks like a cross-reference to MALARKEY, but it is just anagram fodder; 'shot' also fakes filming.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1939 Civil War epic starring Vivien Leigh and Clark Gable is one of Hollywood's most famous films.

clue.text: Beginning to clock husband is a bit overweight

indicators.note: beginning to a word is its first letter

parts.note: first letter of clock
informal word for a husband

explanation.surface: Someone starts to notice that their husband is putting on weight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clock' in British slang means to notice, which drives the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Plump, rounded and slightly fat describes someone carrying a little extra weight.

clue.text: Bill does a twirl, modelling daring garment

indicators.note: a twirl spins round, so the word is turned back to front

parts.note: AC is the abbreviation for account, a bill

indicators.note: modelling means shaping, so these letters are moulded into a new form

parts.note: every letter is used

explanation.surface: A man called Bill spins on the catwalk, modelling a bold item of clothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill' looks like a man's name, but it is an account, AC.
explanation.definitionFit: A knitted woollen jacket fastening down the front is an item of clothing.
